cards.front: What is DNS enumeration, and how is it different from just looking up an A record?
cards.back:
DNS enumeration is the systematic querying of ALL available DNS record types (A, AAAA, MX, NS, TXT, CNAME, PTR, SRV) for a domain and all its subdomains.

Looking up one A record gives you one IP. DNS enumeration gives you:
— The email provider (MX)
— The DNS hosting provider (NS)
— Every cloud vendor in use (TXT verification tokens)
— Whether the domain can be spoofed (DMARC p= value)
— Every CDN and SaaS relationship (CNAME)
— The complete list of subdomains and their IPs

One lookup is a phone number. Enumeration is the complete directory.
cards.hint: DNS has 8 record types. A record is one of them.

cards.front: What does the MX record reveal, and why is a self-hosted MX record significant?
cards.back:
MX (Mail Exchange) record reveals which server receives email for the domain.

aspmx.l.google.com = Google Workspace
mail.protection.outlook.com = Microsoft 365
A company's own hostname = self-hosted mail server

Self-hosted MX is significant because mail servers communicate directly via SMTP — no CDN proxying. The mail server's IP is a real, direct, internet-facing address. Running IP WHOIS on it often reveals the organisation's actual hosting infrastructure — bypassing any CDN protection on the main website.
cards.hint: MX = mail room address. What service runs the mail room?

cards.front: What does the NS record reveal, and why does it matter for security?
cards.back:
NS (Nameserver) record reveals which servers are authoritative for the domain's DNS — the official source of all DNS records.

ns1.cloudflare.com = Cloudflare manages DNS (and likely CDN)
awsdns = AWS Route 53 (infrastructure likely on AWS)
Custom NS = self-managed, possible zone transfer target

Security implication: compromising the account that manages NS records (Cloudflare account, Route 53 account) allows changing all DNS records — redirecting website, email, everything. NS records tell you where the critical DNS management account lives.
cards.hint: NS = management office. Who runs the building's official records?

cards.front: What does a DMARC TXT record p= value tell you, and what does p=none mean?
cards.back:
DMARC (v=DMARC1) controls what happens when an email fails authentication.

p=none = monitoring only — failing emails are DELIVERED ANYWAY. The domain can be spoofed in phishing emails. This is a finding in every professional penetration test report.

p=quarantine = failing emails go to spam. Harder to phish but not impossible.

p=reject = failing emails are rejected entirely. Strongest protection — spoofed emails blocked.

Query: dig TXT _dmarc.target.com
cards.hint: p=none means the door is unlocked — emails can be faked.

cards.front: What is a dangling CNAME, and why is it a security vulnerability?
cards.back:
A dangling CNAME is a DNS CNAME record whose destination domain or cloud resource no longer exists, but the DNS record was never removed.

Example: blog.company.com CNAME company.wpcomstaging.com → company's WordPress account was deleted → NXDOMAIN

If the destination resource can be claimed (register the WordPress subdomain name), the claimant controls what is served from blog.company.com — the company's trusted subdomain.

This is subdomain takeover — serving malicious content from a corporate domain without touching their systems.
cards.hint: A CNAME pointing somewhere that no longer exists = unlocked door.

cards.front: What does a PTR record do, and what does it reveal in reconnaissance?
cards.back:
PTR (Pointer) record is reverse DNS: it maps an IP address to a hostname.

Where A records go name → IP, PTR records go IP → name.

Reconnaissance use: run a PTR lookup on any discovered IP address. The hostname often reveals the server's purpose:
vpn-gw-01.company.com → VPN gateway
db-primary.company.com → primary database server
jenkins.company.com → CI/CD server

PTR records reveal internal naming conventions and server roles — information not always visible in forward DNS.
cards.hint: PTR = reverse phone book. Number → name.

cards.front: What is a DNS zone transfer (AXFR) and what does it reveal when misconfigured?
cards.back:
A zone transfer (AXFR query) copies the complete DNS zone from primary to secondary nameserver for synchronisation. Legitimate between authorised servers.

When misconfigured to accept requests from any IP: it dumps EVERY DNS record in the zone to the requester — all internal hostnames, all IP addresses, all server names, all services.

Command (in authorised engagement): dig axfr @ns1.target.com target.com

IMPORTANT: Zone transfer is an ACTIVE technique — it contacts the target's nameserver directly. Requires written authorisation.
cards.hint: Zone transfer = accidentally handing out the complete building blueprint.

cards.front: Why are development and legacy subdomains often the most valuable reconnaissance findings?
cards.back:
Development and legacy subdomains are high-value targets because:

— They often resolve to direct IPs (no CDN protection)
— They run the same application code as production, but often with older versions
— They are patched less frequently ('it's just dev')
— They are not on anyone's active security monitoring list
— They may contain real credentials in configuration files
— They may have weaker access controls ('it's internal only')

The organisation built and deployed them — then forgot about them. The DNS record stayed. Anyone who does DNS enumeration finds them.

The main website may be impenetrable. The dev subdomain running a two-year-old framework version may not be.
cards.hint: Forgotten branches run old software. Nobody patches what nobody knows is there.
